resources.string: Explore six important differences between mobile and desktop applications. Use each dimension to evaluate an app or feature you are designing.
Enter the name of an application or feature first.
For \"%1$s\", consider how the %2$s dimension should influence your design.
Phone users interact mainly through touch instead of a mouse and keyboard. Fingers are less precise, and users may operate the device with one hand while moving.
Use comfortably sized touch targets, place important actions within easy thumb reach, and reduce typing when selections can collect the same information.
Mobile screens vary in size, orientation, pixel density, and available space. Content that fits one phone may become crowded on another.
Use flexible Compose layouts, dp for interface measurements, and sp for text. Allow content to wrap or scroll instead of using fixed positions.
Android may recreate an activity after rotation or stop an application when memory is needed. Mobile devices also have limited battery and network availability.
Preserve important user progress and avoid unnecessary background work. Release resources when the screen is no longer being used.
A mobile device travels with its user, so conditions such as location, connectivity, motion, time, and lighting can change during a session.
Design useful offline behavior and request contextual information such as location only when the feature genuinely requires it.
People often use mobile applications in short and interrupted sessions while travelling, waiting, or completing another activity.
Make the main task easy to find, reduce the required steps, and allow users to continue from where they previously stopped.
Phones may contain personal messages, photos, location history, and account information. They can also be lost, shared, or stolen.
Request only necessary permissions, explain why information is needed, protect sensitive data, and avoid placing private information in logs.
